verdict: Caution on Chandigarh IT-enabled services & BPO: lend selectively to domestic mid-size BPO/KPO and captives with contracted receivables; avoid small STP-dependent exporters with client concentration.
title: Chandigarh IT-enabled services & BPO: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**An IT-enabled services or BPO unit sells trained seats and process hours, not a product.** Cash comes in as monthly billing per seat or per transaction from a client contract; cash goes out as salaries, rent for the floor, telecom and software licences. **The asset base is thin — desktops, leased premises, and people — so the bank's real security is the receivable stream and the contract, not the fixed assets.** Pricing power is weak: a rating note on a staffing-led peer says competitive pressure limits pricing power and margin expansion [8]. So when a proposal lands, check the client contract tenure and the per-seat rate; if the rate is below the unit's own cost per seat, ask why they are bidding. ## Where cash sits and what has changed
**Working capital is the whole game: receivables net of payables, and the cycle length decides how much funding the unit needs** [10]. Locally, the signal is weak and negative: **Software Technology Park unit count in Chandigarh has dropped from 20 to 13 in two years** [2]. That is a local news report, not a peer result, and it tells us small STP-registered units are exiting. Peer results are mixed: eClerx grew revenue 17.1% YoY to INR 1,212.6 crore in Q2 FY2026-27 [4], while Hinduja Global Solutions' EBITDA margin fell to 11.2% from 19.0% [5]. Large IT firms held margins — TCS at 24%, Infosys at 21% [6] — but that is the listed tier, not Chandigarh SMEs. The data pack gives no city score [D], so I am leaning on first principles and peers. ## Who to pursue now
**Pursue domestic-demand BPO/KPO units and captive back-offices of Indian corporates, where billing is in rupees and contracts renew annually.** Also pursue units doing AI-assisted analytics or digital operations — eClerx's 17.1% growth [4] and the peer note on smaller, faster AI-led deal wins [3] show where the work is moving. **Avoid pure voice-only exporters with one or two overseas clients, and avoid units whose STP registration lapses or whose seat count is falling** [2]. For any new proposal, collect from customer: client-wise revenue share, contract tenure, attrition rate, and receivable days. ## How to grow safely
**Structure as a receivables-backed working capital line, not a term loan** — capex is leased desktops and fit-outs, so fund the cycle, not the furniture. Take monthly: bank statement of the operating account, GST returns, and an ageing of receivables. Covenant on receivable days and on top-client concentration; if concentration crosses the level you set at sanction, ask for a client-wise billing statement before the next drawdown. **Performance guarantees may be needed for bid-based contracts** [10], so size the non-fund limit separately. ## Early-warning signs
**Watch salary payment dates slipping, GST filing gaps, and receivable days stretching beyond the sanctioned cycle** [10]. A falling seat count or a lapsed STP registration [2] is an exit signal. Margin compression like HGS's fall to 11.2% [5] tells you pricing is being conceded — ask for the rate card.
watch: Monthly bank statement and salary debit dates (monthly)
salary paid after the 7th twice in a row -> ask for client payment confirmation and freeze incremental drawdown
receivable days stretch beyond sanctioned cycle -> reprice or reduce limit
Seat count and STP registration status (quarterly)
seat count falls or registration lapses -> treat as exit signal, no renewal
concentration rises above sanction level -> ask for client-wise billing before next drawdown
watch_note: Trigger levels are policy suggestions (analytical framing), not data.
